claim: Direct-to-consumer (DTC) genetics services have tens of millions of customers.
source: Direct-to-consumer (DTC) genetics services are increasingly popular, with tens of millions of customers.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a general fact about the industry size.

claim: An adversary who uploads approximately 900 genomes could recover at least one allele at SNP sites across up to 82% of the genome of a median person of European ancestries.
source: For example, an adversary who uploads approximately 900 genomes could recover at least one allele at SNP sites across up to 82% of the genome of a median person of European ancestries.
evidence: This claim is supported by the IBS tiling analysis presented in the manuscript, specifically shown in Figure 2.

claim: In databases that detect IBS segments using unphased genotypes, approximately 100 falsified uploads can reveal enough genetic information to allow genome-wide genetic imputation.
source: In databases that detect IBS segments using unphased genotypes, approximately 100 falsified uploads can reveal enough genetic information to allow genome-wide genetic imputation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the parallel IBS baiting analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: Over 26 million people are enrolled in the databases of the five largest DTC genetics companies.
source: One of the major applications of DTC genetics is genetic genealogy. Customers of companies such as 23andMe and Ancestry, once they are genotyped, can view a list of other customers who are likely to be genetic relatives. These putative relatives' full names are often given, and sometimes contact details are given as well. Such genealogical matching services are of interest to people who want to find distant genetic relatives to extend their family tree, and can be particularly useful to people who otherwise may not have information about their genetic relatives, such as adoptees or the biological children of sperm donors. Several genetic genealogy services—including GEDmatch, MyHeritage, FamilyTreeDNA, and LivingDNA (Table 1)—allow users to upload their own genetic data if they have been genotyped by another company.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Regalado (2019) in the introduction.

claim: Several genetic genealogy services allow users to upload their own genetic data if they have been genotyped by another company.
source: Several genetic genealogy services—including GEDmatch, MyHeritage, FamilyTreeDNA, and LivingDNA (Table 1)—allow users to upload their own genetic data if they have been genotyped by another company.
evidence: This is stated as a fact and supported by Table 1 which lists these services.

claim: Upload services have been used by law enforcement to identify relatives of the source of a crime-scene sample.
source: Upload services have also been used by law enforcement, with the goal of identifying relatives of the source of a crime-scene sample (Erlich et al., 2018; Edge and Coop, 2019), prompting discussion about genetic privacy (Syndercombe Court, 2018; Ram et al., 2018; Kennett, 2019; Scudder et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Erlich et al., 2018 and Edge and Coop, 2019.

claim: GEDmatch has a database size of 1.2 million individuals.
source: Table 1
evidence: Table 1 shows GEDmatch database size as 1.2 million as of July 26th, 2019.

claim: GEDmatch shows 3000 closest matches for free and unlimited matches with a $10/month license.
source: Table 1
evidence: Table 1 lists the parameters for GEDmatch including the number of individuals shown.

claim: GEDmatch reports IBS/IBD segments if longer than user-set threshold with a minimum threshold of 0.1 cM and default of 7 cM.
source: Table 1
evidence: Table 1 specifies the IBS/IBD segment reporting parameters for GEDmatch.

claim: Pairs of people who share an ancestor in the recent past can share segments of genetic material from that ancestor.
source: Pairs of people who share an ancestor in the recent past can share segments of genetic material from that ancestor.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in population genetics, supported by multiple citations in the manuscript.

claim: Very long IBS segments, say over 7 centiMorgans (cM), are likely to be IBD.
source: Very long IBS segments, say over 7 centiMorgans (cM), are likely to be IBD, but shorter IBS segments, say <4 cM, may or may not represent true IBD due to recent sharing—they may instead represent a mosaic of shared ancestry deeper in the past.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the relationship between IBS segment length and IBD.

claim: Shorter IBS segments (<4 cM) may or may not represent true IBD due to recent sharing.
source: Very long IBS segments, say over 7 centiMorgans (cM), are likely to be IBD, but shorter IBS segments, say <4 cM, may or may not represent true IBD due to recent sharing—they may instead represent a mosaic of shared ancestry deeper in the past.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about IBS and IBD segments.

claim: Many DTC genetics companies give customers information about their shared IBS with each putative relative, possibly including the number, lengths, and locations of shared genetic segments.
source: Many DTC genetics companies, in addition to sharing a list of putative genealogical relatives, give customers information about their shared IBS with each putative relative, possibly including the number, lengths, and locations of shared genetic segments (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated as a fact and supported by Table 1 which details the reporting practices of various services.

claim: Knowing the locations of IBS sharing with putative relatives reveals information about those relatives' genotypes in those locations.
source: This IBS report may represent substantial information about one's putative relatives—one already has access to one's own genotype, and so knowing the locations of IBS sharing with putative relatives reveals information about those relatives' genotypes in those locations (He et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2014 and is a logical inference from the definition of IBS.

claim: Publicly available genotypes from the 1000Genomes Project, Human Genome Diversity Project, OpenSNP project, or similar initiatives might be uploaded by an adversary.
source: Publicly available genotypes from the 1000Genomes Project (Abecasis et al., 2012), Human Genome Diversity Project (Cann et al., 2002), OpenSNP project (Greshake et al., 2014), or similar initiatives might be uploaded.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about what an adversary could do, supported by citations to these public databases.

claim: Artificial genetic datasets can be designed to reveal the genotypes of users at single sites of interest or sufficiently widely spaced sites genome-wide.
source: Such artificial datasets can be designed to reveal the genotypes of users at single sites of interest or sufficiently widely spaced sites genome-wide.
evidence: This claim is supported by the IBS baiting analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: A set of a few hundred artificial datasets could be designed to reveal enough genotype information to allow accurate imputation of common genotypes for every user in the database.
source: We describe how a set of a few hundred artificial datasets could be designed to reveal enough genotype information to allow accurate imputation of common genotypes for every user in the database.
evidence: This is supported by the parallel IBS baiting analysis in the manuscript.

claim: GEDmatch, as of mid-December 2019, was vulnerable to an attack termed IBS baiting that obtains genotype data via artificial data uploads.
source: In particular, we show that GEDmatch, as of mid-December 2019, was vulnerable to an attack we term IBS baiting that obtains genotype data via artificial data uploads.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the proof-of-concept uploads to GEDmatch described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The work of this manuscript is largely complementary to the independent work of Ney et al. (2020), which was first posted publicly within a week of the first public posting of this manuscript on bioRxiv.
source: Our results are largely complementary to the independent work of Ney et al. (2020), which was first posted publicly within a week of the first public posting of this manuscript on bioRxiv.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between two independent research efforts.

claim: Using the entire sample (871 genotypes) and including all called IBS segments >1 cM, the median person has an average of 60% of the maximum length of 2.8 Gbp covered by IBS segments.
source: Using the entire sample (871 genotypes, since the target is left out) and including all called IBS segments >1 cM, the median person has an average of 60% of the maximum length of 2.8 Gbp covered by IBS segments (with the average taken across their two chromosomes), and sites across 82% of this length have at least one of two alleles recoverable by IBS tiling.
evidence: This is a result from the IBS tiling analysis, shown in Figure 2.

claim: Sites across 82% of the genome length have at least one of two alleles recoverable by IBS tiling when using 871 comparison genotypes and including all IBS segments >1 cM.
source: Using the entire sample (871 genotypes, since the target is left out) and including all called IBS segments >1 cM, the median person has an average of 60% of the maximum length of 2.8 Gbp covered by IBS segments (with the average taken across their two chromosomes), and sites across 82% of this length have at least one of two alleles recoverable by IBS tiling.
evidence: This is a result from the IBS tiling analysis, shown in Figure 2.

claim: With a cutoff of 3 cM, approximately 6.9% of the median person's genotype information is recoverable, including at least one of two alleles at sites in 11% of the genome.
source: With a cutoff of 3 cM, approximately 6.9% of the median person's genotype information is recoverable, including at least one of two alleles at sites in 11% of the genome.
evidence: This is a result from the IBS tiling analysis with different cM thresholds.

claim: When a more stringent cutoff of 8 cM is used, only 1% of the genome has at least one of two alleles recoverable for the median person when using a comparison sample of 871.
source: When a more stringent cutoff of 8 cM is used, only 1% of the genome has at least one of two alleles recoverable for the median person when using a comparison sample of 871.
evidence: This is a result from the IBS tiling analysis with different cM thresholds.

claim: Refined IBD sometimes splits long IBS segments into multiple shorter segments in the presence of phasing errors.
source: Our reports for segments longer than 3 cM may be conservative because Refined IBD sometimes splits long IBS segments into multiple shorter segments in the presence of phasing errors (Browning and Browning, 2013; Bjelland et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Browning and Browning, 2013 and Bjelland et al., 2017.

claim: For some people, the top 10% have genotypes across 76% of their total genome covered by IBS tiles, including one or more alleles at sites in at least 93% of the 2.8 Gbp covered by IBS tiles anywhere.
source: In our sample, the top 10% of people have genotypes across 76% of their total genome covered by IBS tiles, including one or more alleles at sites in at least 93% of the 2.8 Gbp covered by IBS tiles anywhere.
evidence: This is a result from the IBS tiling analysis showing variation among individuals.

claim: If only segments longer than 3 cM are reported, the top 10% of people have one or both alleles covered at sites in at least 38% of the total genome.
source: If only segments longer than 3 cM are reported, the top 10% of people have one or both alleles covered at sites in at least 38% of the total, and if only segments longer than 8 cM are reported, the top 10% have one or both alleles covered at sites in at least 6% of the total.
evidence: This is a result from the IBS tiling analysis showing variation among individuals with different cM thresholds.

claim: If only segments longer than 8 cM are reported, the top 10% of people have one or both alleles covered at sites in at least 6% of the total genome.
source: If only segments longer than 3 cM are reported, the top 10% of people have one or both alleles covered at sites in at least 38% of the total, and if only segments longer than 8 cM are reported, the top 10% have one or both alleles covered at sites in at least 6% of the total.
evidence: This is a result from the IBS tiling analysis showing variation among individuals with different cM thresholds.

claim: IBS tiling coverage depends on the specific practices used for reporting IBS information.
source: The coverage obtained by IBS tiling and its informativeness about target genotypes depends on the specific practices used for reporting IBS information (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the various supplementary figures showing different scenarios.

claim: DTC genealogy services may take additional steps to ensure that any short segments reported are likely to be IBD, not merely IBS, which will tend to decrease the amount of IBS tiling possible.
source: For example, DTC genealogy services may take additional steps to ensure that any short segments reported are likely to be IBD, not merely IBS. Such steps will tend to decrease the amount of IBS tiling possible, particularly for short segments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1 which shows reduced tiling with higher LOD score thresholds.

claim: Some DTC genealogy services only report matching segments for pairs of people who share at least one long IBS segment, but then allow users to see shorter IBS segments for those pairs of people.
source: As another example, some DTC genealogy services only report matching segments for pairs of people who share at least one long IBS segment (Table 1), but then allow users to see shorter IBS segments (>1cM) for those pairs of people.
evidence: This is stated as a fact and supported by Table 1.

claim: The strategy of requiring at least one long IBS match before reporting any IBS segments allows a higher level of IBS tiling than if only long segments are revealed.
source: Unsurprisingly, we find that this strategy allows a higher level of IBS tiling than if only long segments are revealed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), because people who share a long IBS segment may also share shorter segments that are hidden if only long segments are reported.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Most genetic genealogy services that provide information on the location of IBS matches with putative relatives do not provide haplotype information.
source: Most genetic genealogy services that provide information on the location of IBS matches with putative relatives do not provide haplotype information, making it difficult to distinguish IBS1 (in which one chromosome is covered by an IBS segment) and IBS2 (in which both chromosomes are covered by IBS segments).
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about current practices.

claim: One tool available to an adversary pursuing IBS tiling is to upload genotype information that is homozygous at all sites using one of two phased haplotypes as a basis, effectively searching for IBS with one chromosome at a time.
source: One tool available to an adversary pursuing IBS tiling is to upload genotype information that is homozygous at all sites using one of two phased haplotypes as a basis, effectively searching for IBS with one chromosome at a time.
evidence: This is a proposed method based on inference about how IBS detection works.

claim: IBS tiling rates vary somewhat by population, with Finnish samples showing the highest tiling rates among the 1000Genomes populations included.
source: IBS tiling rates vary somewhat by population, with Finnish samples showing the highest tiling rates among the 1000Genomes populations included (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: There appear to be slight biases for IBS tiles to appear in regions with low SNP density and lower heterozygosity.
source: There also appear to be slight biases for IBS tiles to appear in regions with low SNP density and lower heterozygosity, meaning that the proportion of alleles—and particularly the proportion of minor alleles—recovered by tiling is typically slightly lower than the proportion of the genome length in Mbp covered (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: By IBS probing, one could identify people with specific genotypes of interest, such as risk alleles for Alzheimer's disease.
source: By IBS probing, one could identify people with specific genotypes of interest, such as risk alleles for Alzheimer's disease (Corder et al., 1993), even if the DTC service does not report chromosomal locations of IBS matches.
evidence: This is a proposed method supported by the demonstration in Figure 3 and citations.

claim: To identify people carrying a particular allele at a locus of interest, one could use haplotypes carrying the allele in publicly available databases.
source: To identify people carrying a particular allele at a locus of interest, one could use haplotypes carrying the allele in publicly available databases.
evidence: This is a proposed method based on inference.

claim: One simple way of generating chromosomes unlikely to have long shared segments with any entries in the database is to sample alleles at each locus in proportion to their frequencies.
source: One simple way is to sample alleles at each locus in proportion to their frequencies.
evidence: This is a proposed method based on inference about population genetics.

claim: Chromosomes generated by sampling alleles in proportion to their frequencies are free of linkage disequilibrium (LD) and thus unlike genuine chromosomes.
source: Chromosomes generated in this way are free of linkage disequilibrium (LD) and thus unlike genuine chromosomes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about LD and how it arises.

claim: With 1-cM matching, 1497 of 1744 haplotypes (86%) matched one of the probes at the site of interest in the APOE locus demonstration.
source: With 1-cM matching, 1497 of 1744 haplotypes (86%) matched one of the probes at the site of interest.
evidence: This is a result from the IBS probing demonstration shown in Figure 3.

claim: With 3-cM matching, 164 of 1744 haplotypes (9.4%) matched one of the probes at the site of interest in the APOE locus demonstration.
source: With 3-cM matching, 164 of 1744 haplotypes (9.4%) matched one of the probes at the site of interest.
evidence: This is a result from the IBS probing demonstration shown in Figure 3.

claim: Very few matches occurred outside the region of interest in the IBS probing demonstration—none with a 3-cM threshold and only 0.1% of matches with a 1-cM threshold.
source: Very few matches occurred outside the region of interest—none with a 3-cM threshold and only 0.1% of matches with a 1-cM threshold.
evidence: This is a result from the IBS probing demonstration shown in Figure 3.

claim: The efficacy of IBS probing will depend on the minimum IBS-match length reported to users, the specific methods used for identifying IBS segments, and whether the genotype of interest is included on the SNP chip.
source: The efficacy of IBS probing will depend on the minimum IBS-match length reported to users, the specific methods used for identifying IBS segments (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2), and whether the genotype of interest is included on the SNP chip.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis and supported by supplementary figures.

claim: High thresholds for IBS reporting will mean that uploaded genotypes will need to have long IBS segments with targets at the locus of interest, reducing the sensitivity of IBS probing.
source: For example, high thresholds for IBS reporting will mean that uploaded genotypes will need to have long IBS segments with targets at the locus of interest. Long IBS segments are likely to represent relatively close genealogical relatives (i.e. long IBS segments are likely to be IBD segments), and not many targets will be close relatives of the source of any given haplotype of interest, meaning that the sensitivity of IBS probing is reduced by reporting thresholds that require long IBS segments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between IBS segment length and genealogical relatedness.

claim: If the locus of interest or a highly correlated one is not included on the chip used to genotype either the uploaded sample or the target sample, then probing may only be expected to work well if the upload and the target are truly IBD rather than merely IBS.
source: If the locus of interest or a highly correlated one is not included on the chip used to genotype either the uploaded sample or the target sample, then probing may only expected to work well if the upload and the target are truly IBD rather than merely IBS, reducing the precision of IBS probing for variants that are not genotyped.
evidence: This is an inference based on the difference between IBS and IBD.

claim: IBS probing will perhaps be most sensitive and precise when the allele of interest is both common and relatively young, as is the case for founder mutations.
source: IBS probing will perhaps be most sensitive and precise when the allele of interest is both common and relatively young, as is the case for founder mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on population genetics principles about haplotype sharing.

claim: IBS baiting is possible if the database identifies putative IBS segments by searching for long regions where a pair of people has no incompatible homozygous sites.
source: The specific strategy for IBS baiting that we describe is possible if the database identifies putative IBS segments by searching for long regions where a pair of people has no incompatible homozygous sites.
evidence: This is the basis for the IBS baiting method described and demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: An incompatible homozygous site is a site at which one person in the pair is homozygous for one allele, and the other person is homozygous for the other allele.
source: An incompatible homozygous site is a site at which one person in the pair is homozygous for one allele, and the other person is homozygous for the other allele.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the manuscript.

claim: Phase-unaware methods for IBS detection do not require phased genotypes and scale relatively easily to large datasets.
source: Identifying IBS segments in this way does not require phased genotypes and scales relatively easily to large datasets—we refer to methods in this class as 'phase-unaware' and contrast them with phase-aware methods for IBS detection.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of phase-unaware methods.

claim: Phase-unaware methods are robust to phasing errors, which are an issue for long IBD segments.
source: Phase-unaware methods are robust to phasing errors, which are an issue for long IBD segments (Durand et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Durand et al., 2014.

claim: Major DTC genetics companies have used phase-unaware methods in the past for IBS detection.
source: Major DTC genetics companies have used phase-unaware methods in the past for IBS detection (Henn et al., 2012; Hon et al., 2013), and some state-of-the-art IBD detection and phasing pipelines feature an initial phase-unaware step (Huang et al., 2014; Loh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Henn et al., 2012 and Hon et al., 2013.

claim: Some state-of-the-art IBD detection and phasing pipelines feature an initial phase-unaware step.
source: Major DTC genetics companies have used phase-unaware methods in the past for IBS detection (Henn et al., 2012; Hon et al., 2013), and some state-of-the-art IBD detection and phasing pipelines feature an initial phase-unaware step (Huang et al., 2014; Loh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2014 and Loh et al., 2016.

claim: The main tool used in IBS baiting is the construction of apparently IBS segments by assigning every uploaded site in the region to be heterozygous.
source: The main tool used in IBS baiting is the construction of apparently IBS segments by assigning every uploaded site in the region to be heterozygous.
evidence: This is the key method described for IBS baiting.

claim: Runs of heterozygosity are unlikely to occur naturally, unlike runs of homozygosity.
source: These runs of heterozygosity, which are unlikely to occur naturally (unlike runs of homozygosity, [McQuillan et al., 2008; Pemberton et al., 2012]), will be identified as IBS with every genome in the database using phase-unaware methods: because they contain no homozygous sites at all, they cannot contain homozygous sites incompatible with any person in the database.
evidence: This is supported by citations to McQuillan et al., 2008 and Pemberton et al., 2012.

claim: Runs of heterozygosity will be identified as IBS with every genome in the database using phase-unaware methods because they contain no homozygous sites at all.
source: These runs of heterozygosity, which are unlikely to occur naturally (unlike runs of homozygosity, [McQuillan et al., 2008; Pemberton et al., 2012]), will be identified as IBS with every genome in the database using phase-unaware methods: because they contain no homozygous sites at all, they cannot contain homozygous sites incompatible with any person in the database.
evidence: This is an inference based on the definition of phase-unaware IBS detection.

claim: Users' genotypes at any single biallelic site of interest can be determined by examining their putative IBS with each of two artificial datasets in single-site IBS baiting.
source: If IBS is identified by looking for single incompatible homozygous sites and missing data can be ignored, then users' genotypes at any single biallelic site of interest can be determined by examining their putative IBS with each of two artificial datasets (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the single-site IBS baiting method described and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: For any genotyped biallelic site of interest, the genotypes of every user shown as a match can be revealed after uploading two artificial datasets in single-site IBS baiting.
source: Thus, for any genotyped biallelic site of interest, the genotypes of every user shown as a match can be revealed after uploading two artificial datasets.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the single-site IBS baiting method.

claim: Genotypes of medical interest that are often included in SNP chips, such as those in the APOE locus, are potentially vulnerable to single-site IBS baiting.
source: Genotypes of medical interest that are often included in SNP chips, such as those in the APOE locus (Corder et al., 1993), are potentially vulnerable to single-site IBS baiting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the single-site IBS baiting method and supported by citation.

claim: If IBS segments as short as 1 cM are reported to the user, then accurate imputation (97–98% accuracy) becomes possible after comparison with only about 100 uploaded datasets in parallel IBS baiting.
source: If IBS segments as short as 1 cM are reported to the user, then accurate imputation (97–98% accuracy) becomes possible after comparison with only about 100 uploaded datasets.
evidence: This is based on the parallel IBS baiting method and citation to Shi et al., 2018 about imputation accuracy.

claim: With a minimum reported IBS threshold of 1 cM, 100 uploaded datasets could reveal approximately 100 genotypes per cM, which is enough to impute genome-wide genotypes at 97-98% accuracy.
source: This means that with a minimum reported IBS threshold of 1 cM, 100 uploaded datasets could reveal approximately 100 genotypes per cM, which is enough to impute genome-wide genotypes at 97 - 98% accuracy (Shi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on the parallel IBS baiting method and citation to Shi et al., 2018.

claim: IBS segments identified by GEDMatch seem to terminate only on incompatible homozygous sites, as would be expected if they use phase-unaware IBS detection.
source: GEDmatch provides no public documentation of the IBS algorithm they use, but IBS segments identified by GEDMatch seem to terminate only on incompatible homozygous sites, as would be expected if they use phase-unaware IBS detection.
evidence: This is an inference based on observation of GEDmatch behavior.

claim: The GEDmatch 1-to-1 match tool identifies the locations of IBS segments between pairs of genetic datasets and allows the user to specify the minimum genetic length and minimum number of matching SNPs to include in a segment.
source: Specifically, the GEDmatch 1-to-1 match tool identifies the locations of IBS segments between pairs of genetic datasets ('kits' in GEDMatch terminology) and allows the user to specify the minimum genetic length and minimum number of matching SNPs to include in a segment.
evidence: This is a description of GEDmatch functionality based on observation.

claim: The GEDmatch 1-to-1 tool returns a 'full resolution' picture of the chromosome that appears to be a SNP-by-SNP picture of the match between the kits along each chromosome.
source: The 1-to-1 tool also returns a 'full resolution' picture of the chromosome that appears to be a SNP-by-SNP picture of the match between the kits along each chromosome.
evidence: This is a description of GEDmatch functionality based on observation.

claim: The full resolution pictures provided by GEDmatch are a major security risk.
source: (These pictures are themselves a major security risk. We alerted GEDmatch to the risk in a July 24th email (posted here: https://github.com/mdedge/IBS_privacy/blob/master/IBS_baiting_demo/GEDmatch_emails.pdf) but did not analyze them further. Ney et al. (2020) showed in detail that the images provided by GEDmatch allow an adversary to learn the full genotype of a target person).
evidence: This is supported by the work of Ney et al. (2020) as cited.

claim: Ney et al. (2020) showed in detail that the images provided by GEDmatch allow an adversary to learn the full genotype of a target person.
source: Ney et al. (2020) showed in detail that the images provided by GEDmatch allow an adversary to learn the full genotype of a target person).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ney et al. (2020).

claim: The authors uploaded artificial genotypes to GEDmatch's research mode beginning in late November 2019 to demonstrate IBS baiting.
source: To demonstrate IBS baiting in GEDmatch, we uploaded a small number of artificial genotypes to their database beginning in late November 2019.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the demonstration.

claim: Before uploading any data to GEDmatch, the authors confirmed their planned procedure with the UC Davis IRB and with GEDmatch representatives.
source: Before uploading any data to GEDmatch, we first confirmed our planned procedure with the UC Davis IRB and with GEDmatch representatives.
evidence: This is a description of the ethical procedures followed.

claim: The authors uploaded their kits into the GEDmatch 'research' and not 'public' category to prevent matches to the public database.
source: We uploaded our kits into the GEDmatch 'research' and not 'public' category to prevent matches to the public database, and only used the 1-to-1 IBS match tool among our own uploaded test kits.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used to avoid interacting with real user data.

claim: The authors avoided interacting with any genotype data of real GEDmatch users and did not violate GEDmatch's terms and conditions.
source: In this way, we avoided interacting with any genotype data of real GEDmatch users and did not violate GEDmatch's terms and conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about the ethical conduct of the research.

claim: In each case of the GEDmatch demonstration, the two bait kits had the correct IBS patterns with the target kits, allowing correct determination of the target genotypes by IBS baiting.
source: In each case, our two bait kits had the correct IBS patterns with the target kits, allowing correct determination of the target genotypes by IBS baiting.
evidence: This is a result from the GEDmatch demonstration shown in Figure 5.

claim: The target and bait kits displayed in Figure 5 were uploaded and analyzed on December 15, 2019, showing that GEDmatch has remained vulnerable to IBS-baiting attacks even after its acquisition by Verogen.
source: The target and bait kits displayed in Figure 5 were uploaded and analyzed on December 15, 2019, showing that GEDmatch has remained vulnerable to IBS-baiting attacks even after its acquisition by Verogen, which was announced on December 9, 2019.
evidence: This is a statement about the timing of the demonstration and GEDmatch's continued vulnerability.

claim: IBS tiling works because there are background levels of IBS (and IBD) even among distantly related members of a population.
source: In particular, IBS tiling works simply because there are background levels of IBS (and IBD) even among distantly related members of a population (e.g. Ralph and Coop, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ralph and Coop, 2013.

claim: IBS tiling performance will depend on the ancestries of the target and comparison samples because IBD rates differ within and among populations.
source: IBS tiling performance will also depend on the ancestries of the target and comparison samples because IBD rates differ within and among populations (Palamara et al., 2012; Carmi et al., 2013; Ralph and Coop, 2013), as well as on the prevalence of close biological relatives in the dataset.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Palamara et al., 2012, Carmi et al., 2013, and Ralph and Coop, 2013.

claim: IBS tiling performance improves as the size of the comparison sample increases.
source: IBS tiling performance improves as the size of the comparison sample increases.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 2 which shows increasing coverage with larger comparison sample sizes.

claim: IBS probing could be used to reveal sensitive genetic information about database participants even if chromosomal locations of matches are not reported to users.
source: As such, IBS probing could be used to reveal sensitive genetic information about database participants even if chromosomal locations of matches are not reported to users.
evidence: This is an inference based on the IBS probing method.

claim: IBS baiting exploits phase-unaware IBS calling algorithms that use incompatible homozygous sites to delimit putative IBS regions.
source: Finally, IBS baiting exploits phase-unaware IBS calling algorithms that use incompatible homozygous sites to delimit putative IBS regions.
evidence: This is a summary of the IBS baiting method.

claim: Approximately 100 well-designed uploads could reveal enough genotypes to impute genome-wide information for any user in a database, provided that the threshold for reporting a matching segment is approximately 1 cM.
source: Although such methods can be useful in genetic genealogy because they scale well to large data, they are vulnerable to fake datasets that include runs of heterozygous sites, which will be identified as IBS with everyone in the database. By inserting homozygous genotypes at key sites and heterozygotes everywhere else, we estimate that approximately 100 well-designed uploads could reveal enough genotypes to impute genome-wide information for any user in a database, provided that the threshold for reporting a matching segment is approximately 1 cM.
